`configs/harness_configs.json` is a new checked-in file naming the harness configs a scheduled run can evaluate. Each entry carries a `name`, an `is_nightly` flag and the run line's own `--ak` kwargs, with the same defaults an unset kwarg has -- so `default` (the `anthropic` lane and nothing else) drives the product exactly as it ships, while `haiku`, `pi-haiku`, `pi-gpt-5-mini`, `pi-glm-4.7-flash` and `opus-standard` name a model and an effort. `default`, `haiku` and `pi-gpt-5-mini` are nightly; the rest run only when a dispatch names them, so which arms cost money every night is a decision recorded in the file. The file's order is the order the cells are decided in, and so the order of the report grid's columns -- which is why arms worth reading against each other, `haiku` beside `pi-haiku`, are listed side by side. A name matches `^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9.-]*$`, is at most 30 characters, is unique and is never `oracle`, because it labels a job, a concurrency group, an artifact and a line of the report; dots are in the pattern because a model version is part of what names an arm (`pi-glm-4.7-flash`), and all four of those take one. Every entry is validated through the driver's own kwarg parsing whether or not it is selected, so a config the driver would refuse at construction is refused on the free resolve job before a paid runner starts, and a unit test validates the checked-in file on every test run. The kwargs of an entry are also the flags to append to a `just minds-evals-run` line to drive the same arm locally.

New `minds-evals ci-matrix`: decides which arms a scheduled run evaluates -- every frozen (mngr, dwt) pair times every selected harness config, minus the cells whose green marker says that exact arm was already verified. It reads the frozen pairs, the harness configs file, the selection (empty selects the nightly set), and the green markers a run may restore, and writes the decided matrix as JSON plus a step-summary table: which pairs run, which cells run, each cell's run line, and each cell's marker key. The key is `minds-evals-green-<pair>-mngr-<sha>-dwt-<sha>-cfg-<config slug>-hc-<config name>-<digest>`, whose digest is over the parsed kwargs, so editing a config re-runs its own cells under the same name and leaves the rest green. `--force` runs every cell regardless. A selection naming a config the file does not hold, or naming nothing at all, is refused rather than deciding an empty matrix, and every kwarg value is held to a shape that survives the run line it rides on.

New `minds-evals ci-report`: renders a scheduled run's Slack report as Block Kit, one message per pair, and writes them as a JSON array of webhook payloads. A message is a header naming the pair and its verdict -- the worst of the pair's oracle pass and its cells: passed, failed, skipped (already green), not evaluated, or broken -- then a line carrying the pair's refs, SHAs, oracle verdict, duration and trigger, then a grid of case by harness config. A grid cell places the trial's reward on an absolute scale as a coloured square (red under 0.25, orange under 0.50, yellow under 0.75, green at or above it), followed by the reward and, where the trial did not complete, failed a gate, left evidence unmeasured or answered on a model other than the one requested, a bold cross. A pass that was never attempted reads `:heavy_minus_sign:`, and `:grey_question:` marks a pass whose summary is missing or unreadable, or a case a graded column has no trial for. A legend under the grid states the bands and the cross, derived from the bands themselves so the two cannot drift apart. The message posts under `:big_brain:` when every arm it reports came out green -- every cell passed, every cell was skipped as already green, or an oracle-only run's oracle passed -- and under `:brainless:` for anything else, the message of a run that decided nothing included. The icon is read off the same verdict the header spells out, so the avatar in the channel list and the words in the message cannot disagree; a run whose arms all passed but whose job went red keeps the green one, because the icon answers "are the arms good?" and the message's own warning is what says the job broke.

Under the grid, the trials that did not pass are listed in a table of config, case and the reason `check-run` recorded. It is drawn only when something failed, so a green run carries no empty heading. Below it one collapsed container, `judge scores`, holds every graded trial of the pair in a single table: config, case, reward, a column per judge criterion, and the trial's state. The criteria are the union across every arm, so a criterion only one config was scored on still gets a column and the arms that were not scored on it print `-` rather than a zero, and a criterion can be compared straight down its own column. The dimensions are stated once in a legend above the table -- `quality: conciseness`, `outcome: works_as_expected` -- rather than in every heading, and a pair scored on more than the 16 criteria a Slack table row leaves room for shows the first 16 and says so. The details block is left with what belongs to no single arm: each skipped, broken or not-evaluated cell, the failing trials of a failed oracle that has no column of its own, and every passing arm whose requested model nothing confirmed. It is budgeted to what a Slack section holds and cut on a line boundary; links to the run's logs and artifacts close the message.

The report uses only the blocks an incoming webhook accepts. A webhook refuses `data_table` outright -- a minimal one is answered with `400 invalid_blocks` -- so the sorting, filtering and paging a data table would bring are unavailable until the notify job posts as an app with a bot token rather than through a webhook; `markdown` is refused as well.

Every message also carries a plain mrkdwn rendering of itself for wherever the blocks do not render, with the grid, the failures and the judge table as fixed-width fences. Those fences say `ok`, `FAIL`, `-` and `?` in place of the emoji, because Slack renders no emoji inside a fence, and the judge fence states the criteria of each dimension on the line above it rather than qualifying every heading. The command is the whole notification of a run, so it never fails: a matrix it cannot read or a summary that is missing is reported as such and the exit code is zero either way.
